title: Volume 10 · Continuity: Backups, Staging and Upgrades
subtitle: Lessons 1–10: the restore drill you can evidence, a staging site that earns its keep, and an upgrade calendar with a rollback
outcomes: Specify and witness a restore drill instead of trusting that backups exist
Define staging that mirrors production closely enough to test an upgrade on
Run a twenty-minute post-upgrade verification that covers print formats, workflows and e-Invoice
Write a version register and an upgrade calendar the client can own without you
Leave a continuity section in the handover pack that survives the next staff change

slides.title: Continuity is a deliverable, not an afterthought
bullets: A functional consultant does not administer servers, but does specify what continuity must look like
The test is simple: how long until the business is trading again, and who is allowed to decide
An untested backup is a rumour; a restore drill you watched is evidence you can sign
Write the requirement into the handover pack with a name and a frequency against each item
Client staff change; a written continuity section is what survives the change

rows: Hours, not days, stated in writing
Dated drill report in the project folder

slides.notes: Say the quiet part early: nobody in the room wants to talk about backups until the day they need one, and by then it is too late to discover the drill was never run. Your job is to turn continuity from a promise into a dated exercise with a name against it. Two sentences in the handover pack, agreed in the last week of the project, prevent the worst conversation of the following year.

slides.title: Database, files and the configuration that is not in either
bullets: A complete backup is the database plus the site's files, which include uploaded documents and private attachments
The database alone restores a site where every invoice printout has a missing attachment
Configuration such as custom fields and print formats lives in the database, but custom apps live in code
The site config carries the database password and encryption key, and it is not in the backup
A backup you cannot restore is worthless, and a restored site without its encryption key is damaged

rows: Open the hosting console for the site
Site list with the Seri Murni instance
Contains db password and encryption key
Store the key outside the backup
Key retrievable by someone other than the DBA

slides.notes: This is where a functional consultant earns their place in a technical conversation: you are not taking the backup, you are checking that the set is complete and current, and that the encryption key is stored somewhere other than the machine it protects. Ask the hosting provider for the schedule in writing and attach it to the handover pack.

slides.title: Restore into a scratch site and time it
bullets: A restore drill runs into a scratch site, never over production, and it is timed with a stopwatch
The drill is done when someone can log in, open last night's invoice and see the attachment
Record the elapsed time, the person who did it and the date, because that record is the evidence
Run it quarterly and again after any infrastructure change the hosting provider makes
If the drill fails, the finding is not a technical problem, it is a go-live blocker

rows: Create a scratch site on the same host
Restore the latest backup into it
Run migrations if the versions differ
Log in as a real user
Desk opens with the client's data
Open last night's invoice and its attachment
Dated entry in the drill log

slides.notes: Time the drill out loud. The number is the deliverable, because it converts an abstract promise into a business fact the client can plan around: we can be back in under an hour, or we cannot. Attach the dated log to the handover pack, and if the drill has never been run, say so plainly and make it a pre-go-live action rather than a footnote.

slides.title: A site you are allowed to break
bullets: Staging is a second site with production-like data where upgrades, patches and customisations are tested first
A staging site with no data proves nothing, because half the failures are in the data, not the code
Restore a production backup into staging before each upgrade so the test is honest
Anything tested on production is a change you are making while the business is trading
Staging is not a luxury line item; it is the cheapest insurance in the project

rows: Same custom fields and print formats

slides.notes: The argument that wins this line item is arithmetic: one upgrade tested on production during a stock take costs more than a staging site for a year. Restore production data into staging before each upgrade, and keep production credentials out of it, because a staging site that can send live e-Invoices is a liability rather than a rehearsal.

slides.title: Pin what you run and schedule when it changes
bullets: Record the exact Frappe, ERPNext and custom app versions at go-live in a version register
Pin those versions so an unannounced update does not change behaviour during a busy week
Plan upgrades on a calendar with a business-quiet window, not on the day a patch appears
Review the changelog before upgrading for renamed fields and deprecated features
Every upgrade has a named approver and a rollback point, even when nothing goes wrong

rows: Version register in the handover pack
Notes attached to the upgrade request

slides.notes: The version register is the document you will be grateful for a year later when a client reports behaviour that no longer matches the course or the manual. Pin, schedule, read the changelog, approve by name, and take the backup immediately before the upgrade so the rollback point is minutes old rather than a night old.

slides.title: The five things an upgrade disturbs
bullets: Print formats are the most common casualty, especially custom HTML that references a renamed field
Custom apps and patches may need a migration step or a version bump of their own
Workflows change when states or actions are renamed, and documents can strand mid-flow
Reports built on specific field names fail quietly by returning nothing rather than an error
e-Invoice submission credentials and endpoints must be re-checked, particularly sandbox versus production

rows: Invoice PDF with logo and terms
No error banner on the Desk
Test a document through every state

slides.notes: This list is the difference between an upgrade and an outage. Print formats break first and most visibly, because clients print invoices before they read reports. Workflows break quietly, stranding documents in a state nobody can move. Reports break silently, returning nothing. Test all five deliberately rather than waiting for the client to discover them one by one.

slides.title: A post-upgrade verification you can hand to the client
bullets: Twenty minutes, five checks, one sign-off: that is the whole ritual and it must be repeatable
Do it on staging first, then repeat on production immediately after the upgrade window
Write the result into the upgrade ticket so the next person can see what was verified and when
A check that cannot be repeated by client staff is not a check, it is your private habit
Attach the checklist to the handover pack with the name of whoever is qualified to run it

rows: Log in as a normal user, not administrator
Desk loads without an error banner
Create and submit a test invoice
Stock and ledger rows appear as usual
PDF renders with logo, terms and totals
Accepted or validated, no credential error
Sign the ticket with time and name

slides.notes: Twenty minutes is the whole cost, and it converts an upgrade from an act of faith into a checked procedure. Insist that a normal user, not the administrator, performs the login step, because permission issues hide from administrator accounts. Then get the ticket signed, so the next upgrade starts from evidence rather than assumption.

slides.title: Where compliance meets continuity
bullets: e-Invoice submission depends on credentials, endpoints and a working outbound connection, all outside the ledger
After any upgrade, submit one document in sandbox before allowing production submissions to resume
Keep a written fallback: manual submission through MyInvois portal within the statutory window
Never store production e-Invoice credentials in staging or in a backup taken for testing
A refused submission after an upgrade is a compliance event, so it belongs in the upgrade checklist

rows: Email or queue visible in the Desk

slides.notes: The compliance dimension is what makes continuity more than housekeeping. A batch of refused e-Invoices after a quiet upgrade is a statutory problem with a deadline, not an inconvenience. Test one submission in sandbox, confirm the production endpoint has not been switched, and write the manual fallback down with a name against it.

slides.title: The plan you hope never to use
bullets: A rollback plan is a backup taken immediately before the change plus a written way to restore it
Decide in advance who may call a rollback and how long the decision may take
Restoring a backup discards transactions made after it, so the window must be planned, not improvised
Rehearse the decision, not just the command: the technical step is easy, the business call is not
If the rollback needs a person who is on leave, the plan is not finished

rows: Take a backup immediately before the upgrade
Archive with a timestamp minutes old
Note the transactions made during the window
A short, known list of documents
Agree the decision maker and the cut-off time
If triggered, restore the pre-upgrade backup
Site returns to the recorded state
Documents restored from the recorded list
Dated note in the handover pack

slides.notes: Rollbacks fail for organisational reasons far more often than technical ones: nobody agreed who could call it, so an hour passes while people discuss. Fix that in the ticket — one name, one cut-off time — and make sure the pre-upgrade backup is taken minutes before the change, not the night before, so the transactions to replay are a short list rather than a day of trading.

slides.title: What goes in the continuity section
bullets: Backup schedule, drill log with dates and elapsed times, and the owner of each
Version register with the pinned numbers and the date they were last confirmed
Upgrade calendar, approval name and the twenty-minute verification checklist
The e-Invoice fallback route, with the person who may execute it and the statutory window
A one-page index so the next consultant or the client's IT can find all of it in a minute
slides.notes: Close the volume where you opened it: continuity is a document someone else can act on. If the client's IT can pick up this section and run a drill without calling you, the project is finished in the way that matters. Read the index out loud in the final session, hand it over on paper as well as in the repository, and name the person responsible for each line.

lab.title: Lab · Evidence continuity for Seri Murni in one afternoon
steps: Inspect the hosting console and record the backup schedule, retention and whether files are included
Download the latest backup set and confirm the timestamps match last night's schedule
Create a scratch site, restore the set into it and time the restore with a stopwatch
Log in as a normal user, open last night's invoice and confirm the attachment opens
Write the drill entry: date, elapsed minutes, person, and what failed if anything did
Take a production backup into staging, run any available patch on staging, then execute the five checks
Switch the e-Invoice endpoint to sandbox and submit one document, then confirm production credentials are untouched
Complete the version register, the upgrade calendar with an approver, and the one-page index for the handover pack
lab.done: A dated drill log with an elapsed time, a staging site restored from production, a signed twenty-minute verification, and a continuity section the client's IT could follow without you.

quiz.question: Why is a nightly backup that has never been restored not evidence of continuity?
options: Because backups are only valid for thirty days
Because nobody knows whether it restores, how long it takes or whether files and the encryption key are usable
Because ERPNext backups exclude the database
Because hosting providers do not keep backups
quiz.why: A backup is a hypothesis until a drill proves it. The drill produces the two facts that matter: the restore works, and the business can be trading again in a known number of minutes.

quiz.question: What must be stored separately from the backup itself?
options: The chart of accounts
The site encryption key, without which a restored site cannot read encrypted data
The print formats
The list of saved filters
quiz.why: The site configuration holds the database password and the encryption key, and it is not inside the backup. Losing the key leaves a restored site unable to decrypt data it still holds.

quiz.question: Why does staging need production-like data rather than an empty site?
options: Because empty sites cannot be upgraded
Because many failures depend on the data and configuration, not the code
Because staging must be licensed separately
Because reports need rows to render
quiz.why: Custom fields, print formats, workflow states and real document shapes are where upgrades break. An empty staging site tests the code path only, which is the smallest part of the risk.

quiz.question: Which artefact usually breaks first after an upgrade, and most visibly?
options: The General Ledger report
Custom print formats, especially those referencing renamed fields
The chart of accounts
User permissions
quiz.why: Print formats are HTML that names fields directly, so a renamed field turns an invoice PDF into an error or a blank. Clients print invoices before they read reports, which makes it the first visible failure.

quiz.question: What makes a rollback plan genuinely usable?
options: A script that restores the last nightly backup
A backup taken minutes before the change, a named decision maker and a cut-off time
A support ticket with the hosting provider
A documented list of every change made since go-live
quiz.why: Rollbacks fail organisationally more often than technically. A backup minutes old keeps the replay list short, and a named decision maker with a cut-off time stops an hour being lost to discussion.

memory.spine: Pin the versions, prove the restore, test on staging, and let one named person approve the upgrade.

device.label: Backup, prove, stage, pin
expansion: Backup, and store the encryption key somewhere the backup cannot reach
Prove it with a timed restore drill into a scratch site, logged with a date
Stage the upgrade on a site holding production-like data, never on production itself
Pin the versions, schedule the window, and review the changelog before the change
One named approver, one cut-off time, and a twenty-minute verification afterwards

cards.q: What two facts does a restore drill give the client?
cards.a: That the backup actually restores, and how many minutes the business needs before it can trade again. Both belong in the handover pack.

cards.q: Why does staging need a copy of production data?
cards.a: Upgrades break on custom fields, print formats and workflow states, which live in the data and configuration rather than in the code.

cards.q: What belongs in the version register?
cards.a: The exact Frappe, ERPNext and custom app versions, pinned at go-live, with the date each was last confirmed and who confirmed it.

cards.q: Which five checks make up the post-upgrade verification?
cards.a: Log in as a normal user, submit a test invoice, print it, run two saved reports, and submit one e-Invoice in sandbox.

cards.q: What makes a rollback plan usable rather than aspirational?
cards.a: A backup taken minutes before the change, a named decision maker, a cut-off time, and a short recorded list of transactions to replay.

trap.what: The client says 'the hosting provider handles backups' and signs off go-live without a drill.
trap.why: Handled is not proven. Ask for the schedule in writing, run one timed restore into a scratch site, log the result, and make an unproven restore a go-live blocker rather than a footnote.

narration: Volume ten ends where most projects are weakest: what happens after go-live, on the day something breaks. Continuity is a consultant deliverable even though the commands belong to somebody else. Pin the versions you went live on and write them in a register. Check with the hosting provider that the nightly backup includes files, and store the site encryption key somewhere the backup cannot reach, because a restored site without its key cannot read what it holds. Then prove it: restore into a scratch site, time it with a stopwatch, log the elapsed minutes with a date and a person, and attach that log to the handover pack. Before every upgrade, restore production data into staging and test there, because print formats, workflows and saved reports break on data and configuration, not just code. Keep one named approver and a cut-off time so a rollback decision takes minutes rather than an argument. Afterwards, twenty minutes of verification: log in as a normal user, submit a test invoice, print it, run two saved reports, and submit one e-Invoice in sandbox. Then sign the ticket and hand the whole section over.
